text: Application code gets reviewed before it merges — a teammate reads the diff and says yes or no. Infrastructure code deserves the same discipline, but a raw dot-tf diff doesn't actually tell a reviewer what will happen in the cloud. One changed argument can mean create one resource, or destroy and recreate twelve. This lesson automates terraform plan so the real answer shows up right on the pull request, before anyone merges.

The trigger is what makes this automatic: on pull_request fires the job every time a PR is opened or updated, no one has to remember to run anything by hand. permissions sets pull-requests to write, which matters later in the job — without it, plan still runs fine, but the workflow won't be allowed to post a comment back. Then actions/checkout pulls the repository onto the runner, and hashicorp/setup-terraform installs the CLI itself.

After terraform init downloads the providers, the plan step runs terraform plan with id: plan, which lets a later step reference its output by name. continue-on-error: true is the detail that matters most here: a plan that fails — a bad variable, a provider error — still needs to show up as a comment on the PR instead of just stopping the job silently before anyone sees why.

actions/github-script turns that captured output into a real comment, using the same GitHub API a human would call by hand. github.rest.issues.createComment posts straight onto the pull request that triggered the workflow — a pull request is a GitHub issue under the hood, which is why the issues API is what posts it. A final status step checks steps.plan.outcome and fails the check if the plan itself errored, since continue-on-error kept that error from stopping the job earlier.

Put together, that's the whole payoff: the reviewer sees the real plan, not a guess at what a diff implies. No apply runs unattended here — this workflow only plans — so there's no surprise before anyone approves anything. And infrastructure changes now get exactly the review discipline application code already gets, reading the actual proposed change instead of trusting that a small-looking diff is actually small.

Posting the plan was the easy half of the problem. The harder question is what happens on the other side of that review — once a PR is approved and merged, should terraform apply just run automatically? Lesson 26 says no, and shows the real gate that stops it from running unattended.
